title: Council opposes Bill 23 and funds planning response
subtitle: Bill 109 planning fees and staffing, development charge shortfalls, heritage and wetland protections, and calls for provincial funding
overview: Council held a special meeting to respond to two provincial laws: Bill 109, which shortens development application timelines and requires fee refunds when they are missed, and Bill 23, which changes development charges, parkland dedication, heritage listings, conservation authority roles and wetland rules. Council first amended the staff recommendation so that it states opposition to Bill 23 in its current form {{vote:m2}}, then approved the full package as amended {{vote:m3}}.

In practical terms, planning and development fees will be updated as an interim step, a full fee review will happen in 2023, and Council approved $1,010,000 for staffing and a fee study. Most of it is one-time money from a contingency reserve, and the rest affects the tax levy. Staff will use the report's themes in the provincial consultations.

Council also asked the Province for longer comment periods, ongoing funding for Bill 109 costs, and funding to cover the growth-infrastructure gap Bill 23 would create. Staff warned that lost development charge revenue could mean higher property taxes and utility rates, or delayed infrastructure. Council also asked the Province to review policies on approved housing that remains unbuilt.

decisions.detail: Council amended the motion so that it states opposition to Bill 23 in its current form, alongside the request for more time to comment.
Council asked the Province to extend 30- and 31-day comment postings to 66 days, and directed staff to use the report's key themes in responding to the Bill 23 consultations.
The planning and development fees by-law will be amended as an interim step to protect fee revenue, and staff will carry out a full fee review in 2023 aiming for full cost recovery.
Council approved $1,010,000 for staffing, related costs and a fee study in 2023, funded by one-time reserve money and a tax levy impact.
Council called on the Province to fund ongoing Bill 109 compliance costs not recovered through fees and to fund the gap between growth infrastructure costs and revenue under Bill 23.
Council asked the Province to review policies and penalties for approved housing units left unbuilt 18 months or more after building permits or zoning approvals.
The report and related public correspondence will be sent to the Premier, the housing minister, a provincial committee, municipal associations and other named bodies.

debate: Staff said the Bill 23 changes to development charges, parkland dedication and community benefits charges would cut growth revenue. They warned the shortfall would fall on property taxes and utility rates, and one finance estimate put the likely effect at a minimum of 2% on top of normal tax increases.

A financial consultant and staff said past cuts to development charges had not been followed by lower housing prices. The consultant also said the changes could limit the city's ability to pay for water and wastewater infrastructure up front.

Many delegates urged Council to reject Bill 23 outright. They raised concerns about local democracy, the loss of wetland and conservation authority oversight, and the dismantling of the heritage register. Others questioned the new definition of affordable housing, which is tied to market prices rather than incomes.

A local builder and a business association representative supported more planning staff and said they wanted to work with the city. The builder said the bill contains no mechanism to make developers pass savings on to buyers. Councillors also asked whether the bill could drive a push for more affordable housing, and staff said it does not require it.

Some councillors wanted a stronger stance, such as a demand that the Province rescind the bill. Staff said a development moratorium is not legally possible and that the city would likely face refunds and appeals. The CAO suggested the stronger test may come when Council decides on the provincial housing pledge.
